column2: In a family where a sinful man is born, bringing all misfortune, he brings only disgrace and buries its fame.
If brothers who are undivided rise up together, a father should never give his sons an unequal share.
He should not slight the eldest, whether wicked or virtuous; if a younger one sees what is better, he should act so, for dharma, say the knowers of dharma, is what is best.
A teacher outweighs ten instructors, a father ten teachers, a mother ten fathers, or even the whole earth.
By her weight she surpasses all; there is no teacher equal to a mother. Because the mother is weightier, people hold her so.
An elder brother, when the father is dead, is equal to a father, O Bharata; he should be their provider and should protect them.
All the younger ones, following his wish, should bow to him and live on him as on a father.
Father and mother create the body, O Bharata; the birth given by the teacher is true, unaging and deathless.
An elder sister is like a mother, O best of the Bharatas, and so is a brother's wife, at whose breast one drank in infancy.
We have heard that brahmins and kshatriyas should keep observances. What is to be done by them in fasting, Grandsire?
O king, tell me the rule for all fasts. What goal does one attain who is devoted to fasting?
Fasting is supreme merit, fasting is the final refuge. Having fasted here, best of men, what fruit does one obtain?
By what is one freed from unrighteousness, how does one gain dharma, and how, best of the Bharatas, does one win heaven and merit?
And what should be given by one who has fasted? Tell me that by which, through dharma, one gains happiness and wealth.
[Vaishampayana] To Kunti's son Yudhishthira, knower of dharma, speaking thus, Bhishma, son of Shantanu, who knew the essence of dharma, said these words.
This was heard of old, great king: the best virtues in the rule of fasting, O best of the Bharatas.
I asked Angiras, the son of Prajapati, rich in austerity, as you have asked me.
A wise man should never be childless or poor; one who wishes to sacrifice should pass the fifth and sixth lunar days fasting and feed brahmins.
Then, O son of Kunti, having fasted on the eighth and the fourteenth of the bright fortnight, he is born free of disease and strong.
One who spends the month of Margashirsha eating once a day and feeds brahmins with devotion is freed from disease and sin.
He is born full of all blessings, possessed of all herbs, sharing in the harvest, wealthy and with many sons.
One who, O son of Kunti, spends the month of Pausha eating once a day is fortunate, good to look at, and a sharer in fame.
A devotee of his ancestors who spends the month of Magha eating once a day attains greatness among his kinsmen in a prosperous family.
One who spends the month of the god Bhaga eating once a day becomes beloved of women, and those women become obedient to him.
One who, self-restrained, spends the month of Chaitra eating once a day is born in a great family rich in gold, jewels and pearls.
A man or woman of mastered senses who passes Vaishakha eating once a day attains pre-eminence among kinsmen.
One who spends the month of Jyeshtha-Mula eating once a day is born, man or woman, to unequalled and supreme lordship.
Staying a month untiring in Ashadha eating once a day, he is born with much grain, wealth and sons.
One who, self-restrained, spends the month of Shravana eating once a day is joined wherever he goes with consecration, and increases his kin.
A man who spends the month of Proshthapada eating one meal attains wealthy, flourishing and steady lordship.
Likewise one who spends the month of Ashvayuja eating once a day is born with offspring, rich in vehicles and with many sons.
A man who keeps one meal a day through the month of Kartika is born brave, with many wives and renowned.
Thus, tiger among men, the months have been told for those who fast; now hear also the rules for the lunar days, O king.
One who eats a meal only once each fortnight, O Bharata, is born rich in cattle, with many sons and long-lived.
Having kept three-night fasts every month for twelve years, he attains lordship over the hosts, without rivals and untroubled.
All these rules should be kept for twelve years, O best of the Bharatas, by one following the path of action.
One who eats morning and evening and drinks nothing between, always devoted to non-harm, offering to Agni Jatavedas,
is perfected in six years, O king, without doubt; he obtains the fruit of the Agnishtoma sacrifice.
In the abode of the apsarases, resounding with dance and song, he mounts a celestial car of the colour of heated gold.
For a full thousand years he is honoured in Brahma's world, and when that is exhausted he returns here and attains greatness.
A man who eats once a day for a full year gains the fruit of the Atiratra sacrifice.
For ten thousand years he is honoured in heaven, and when that is exhausted he returns here and attains greatness.
One who for a full year eats only the fourth meal, always devoted to non-harm, truthful and restrained in senses,
gains the fruit of the Vajapeya sacrifice and is honoured in heaven for thirty thousand years.
A man who, O son of Kunti, passes a year eating at the sixth time gains the fruit of the Ashvamedha sacrifice.
He goes in a car drawn by chakravaka birds and rejoices in heaven for forty thousand years.
A man who lives a year, O king, eating only at the eighth time gains the fruit of the Gavamaya sacrifice.
He goes in a car yoked with swans and cranes and rejoices in heaven for fifty thousand years.
One who, O king, eats once every fortnight for a year, fasts for six months, the blessed Angiras said; and he dwells in heaven for sixty thousand years.
O lord of the people, asleep he is awakened by the sweet, fine sounds of lutes, vallakis and flutes.
A man who for one year drinks only milk every month obtains, dear child, the fruit of the Vishvajit.
He goes in a car drawn by lions and tigers and rejoices in heaven for seventy thousand years.
Beyond a month, tiger among men, fasting is not prescribed; but the knowers of dharma speak, Partha, of a rule of total fasting.
One who goes on a total fast, not in distress and free of disease, gains the fruit of a sacrifice at every step, without doubt.
He goes to heaven in a car yoked with swans, and a hundred apsara maidens delight that man.
One who goes on a total fast, whether in distress or sick, O lord, rejoices in heaven a hundred thousand years, and asleep is awakened by the sound of girdles and anklets.
Having gone in a car bright as the moon and yoked with a thousand swans, he delights, O best of the Bharatas, filled with hundreds of women.
Nourishment is seen for the wasted, healing for the wounded, a store of medicine for the sick, and appeasement for the angry;
giving of goods to the afflicted, and wealth and honour; but these do not please one who desires heaven and is happy-minded.
Therefore, joined with desire, adorned and good, he delights in a golden car filled with hundreds of women.
Healthy, his resolves fulfilled, happy and free of sin, a man who gives up his body fasting obtains the fruit.
In a car like the rising sun, golden-bright, set with beryl and pearls and resounding with lutes and drums,
strewn with banners and lamps, ringing with divine bells and attended by thousands of women, that man prospers happily.
As many as are the pores on his body, O Pandava, so many thousands of years he rejoices in heaven.
There is no scripture higher than the Veda, no teacher like a mother, no gain higher than dharma, and no austerity higher than fasting.
There is nothing more purifying than brahmins, in heaven or here; and no austere act is equal to fasting.
The gods, having fasted by rule, attained heaven, and the sages gained supreme perfection by fasts.
The wise Vishvamitra endured a thousand divine years eating once a day, and by that became a brahmin.
Chyavana, Jamadagni, Vasishtha, Gautama and Bhrigu, all patient great sages, reached heaven.
This was shown of old by Angiras to the great sages; he who always shows it never meets sorrow.
One who reads or always hears this rule, in due order, set forth by the great sage Angiras, O son of Kunti, has no sin.
He is freed from all confusions, his mind is not overcome by faults, he understands the cries of creatures of other wombs, and the best of men gains lasting fame.
Sacrifices, Grandsire, cannot be obtained by the poor; sacrifices need much equipment and are spread with many materials.
They can be obtained by kings and princes, Grandsire, not by those short of means, of few virtues, alone and without allies.
Tell me, Grandsire, the rule that even the poor can always obtain, equal to the fruits of these sacrifices.
[Bhishma] Angiras declared this, with the fruit of fasting as its substance: a rule equal to the fruits of sacrifices. Learn it, Yudhishthira.
One who eats morning and evening and drinks nothing in between, always devoted to non-harm, offering to Agni Jatavedas,
is perfected in six years, without doubt; he obtains a car the colour of heated gold.
In the abode of divine women, resounding with dance and song, he lives in Prajapati's world, fire-bright, for a padma of years.
One who for three years constantly takes only one meal a day, always delighting in his lawful wife, gains the fruit of the Agnishtoma.
Truthful, generous, devoted to brahmins, free of envy, patient, self-controlled and with anger conquered, he goes to the highest goal.
In a car like a pale cloud, marked with swans, he lives with the apsarases for two padmas.
One who eats once on the third day, always for twelve months, offering to Agni Jatavedas,
obtains the supreme fruit of the Atiratra sacrifice, and gets a car yoked with peacocks and swans.
He lives with the apsarases in the world of the seven sages, and his return there is held to be three padmas.
One who eats once on the fourth day, always for twelve months, offering to Agni Jatavedas,
obtains the supreme fruit of the Vajapeya sacrifice and gets a car ridden by Indra's maidens.
At the end of Sagara's time he lives in Vasava's world, and constantly watches the sport of the king of the gods.
One who eats once on the fifth day, always for twelve months, offering to Agni Jatavedas,
free of greed, truthful, devoted to brahmins, harmless, free of envy and of sin, gains the fruit of a twelve-day rite.
He mounts a divine car of gold, marked with swans, bright as a ring of suns, a pale mansion.
Four cycles and twelve padmas, and the measure of the arrows of fire, he lives there happily.
A sage who eats on the sixth day, always for twelve months, offering to Agni Jatavedas,
always bathing three times a day, celibate, without envy, obtains the supreme fruit of the Gavamaya sacrifice.
He attains an excellent vehicle of gold, bright as flame, served by swans and peacocks, well yoked.
Asleep in the lap of the apsarases, he is woken by the sound of anklets and the tinkling of girdles.
For a thousand crore years and three hundred crore, eighteen padmas and two patakas,
and fifty myriads, equal to the number of hairs of a hundred bear-skins, he is honoured in Brahma's world.
One who eats once on the seventh day, always for twelve months, offering to Agni Jatavedas,
guarding Sarasvati, practising celibacy, should avoid flower-colours, honey and meat.
The man goes to the world of the Maruts and the world of Indra, and everywhere, his aims fulfilled, is carried by divine maidens.
He obtains the abundant fruit of the sacrifice of gold, and rejoices in those worlds with a number of years beyond count.
A man who patiently eats on the eighth day for a year, always devoted to the gods' work, offering to Agni Jatavedas,
obtains the supreme fruit of the Paundarika sacrifice and mounts a car with the colour of the lotus.
He gains women dark, golden-fair and brown, playful in youth and beauty, without doubt.
One who eats every ninth day for a year, always for twelve months, offering to Agni Jatavedas,
obtains the fruit of the Ashvamedha sacrifice and gets a car bright as a white lotus.
With the splendour of blazing sun and fire, and with divine garlands, he is borne by Rudra's maidens through the eternal sky.
For eighteen thousand years, and a kalpa, and a hundred thousand crores, he rejoices in those worlds.
One who eats each time ten days have passed, always for twelve months, offering to Agni Jatavedas,
in the abode of Brahma's maidens, delighting all beings, obtains the supreme fruit of a thousand Ashvamedhas.
And beautiful maidens, blue-lotus and red-lotus in hue, always delight that man.
He attains an excellent vehicle, circular and whirling, enclosed with whirls, bright as the waves of the sea.
Resounding with garlands of varied jewels, conches and drums, with crystal and diamond pillars and a well-made altar, he mounts the great car drawn by swans and cranes.
One who eats the oblation-food on the eleventh day, always for twelve months, offering to Agni Jatavedas,
should not desire another's wives in word or in mind, nor speak falsehood, even for his mother and father.
He approaches Mahadeva, the mighty, seated in his car, and sees the Self-existent when his car arrives.
Gold-hued, beautiful maidens lead him to the Rudras' abode in heaven, divine and charming.
For immeasurable years, even to the end of the yuga, and for a hundred thousand crores and ten hundred crores,
he constantly bows to Rudra, honoured by gods and danavas; and each day he comes into his sight.
One who eats the oblation-food on the twelfth day, always for twelve months, gains the fruit of the Sarvamedha.
A car is made for him by the twelve Adityas, adorned with precious jewels, pearls and coral.
It is wreathed with strings of swans, crowded with streets of elephants, and adorned with calling peacocks and chakravakas.
Joined with great towers, it is set in Brahma's world; he dwells there always, O king, surrounded by men and women. So spoke the great sage Angiras, knower of dharma.
One who eats the oblation-food on the thirteenth day, always for twelve months, gains the fruit of a sacrifice of the gods.
A man attains the car called Rising Red Lotus, set with gold, adorned with heaps of red.
Filled with divine maidens, adorned with divine ornaments, rising with holy fragrance, and beautified with airy things.
There he lives to the end of the yuga, a kalpa, a myriad myriads, a padma, and an ocean, with banners and pillars.
With the sound of gandharva songs, the sound of kettledrums and drums, he is always gladdened and praised by those divine maidens.
One who eats the oblation-food on the fourteenth day when complete, always for twelve months, gains the fruit of the Mahamedha.
Divine maidens of indescribable age and beauty, well adorned, wearing polished, heated armlets, follow him in cars.
With the cries of swans, the sound of anklets and the jingle of girdles, he is woken here and there.
A man dwells in the abode of divine maidens, strewn with sands of the Jahnavi, for a full year.
One who, master of his senses, eats one meal when a fortnight has passed, always for twelve months, offering to Agni Jatavedas, obtains the supreme fruit of a thousand Rajasuyas.
He mounts a vehicle served by swans and peacocks, surrounded with circles of jewels and varied gold.
Adorned by excellent women resplendent with divine ornaments, one-pillared, four-doored and seven-storeyed, very auspicious, shining with thousands of banners and with the sounds of song.
He mounts a divine car endowed with divine qualities, adorned with jewels, pearls and coral and bright as lightning, and lives a thousand yugas, riding sword-armed on elephants.
One who eats the oblation-food on the sixteenth day, always for twelve months, gains the fruit of the Soma sacrifice.
He dwells always in the abodes of Soma's maidens, anointed with gentle scents, with movement at will.
He is honoured as he rides in his car by lovely and sweet women, and served with the pleasures of desire.
The fruit is called a hundred padmas, a great kalpa and ten more; that man goes four cycles in the sea.
One who eats the oblation-food on the seventeenth day, always for twelve months,
reaches the realm of Varuna, of Indra and of Rudra, and the realms of the Maruts and of Ushanas, and goes to Brahma's world.
There he is served on a seat by divine maidens, and sees the sage of the gods, Vishvarupa, the earth and sky.
There the maidens of the God of gods delight him, thirty-two in form, sweet and well adorned.
As long as the moon and sun both move in the sky, O lord, so long that hero moves, living on the essence of nectar.
One who eats once on the eighteenth day, always for twelve months, sees the seven worlds.
He is followed from behind by chariots with the sound of Nandi's drums, mounted by divine maidens, shining and well adorned.
Happy indeed, he mounts a divine, excellent car yoked with tigers and lions, resounding like thunder.
There he delights a thousand kalpas with beloved women and enjoys the excellent essence of nectar, like ambrosia.
One who eats once on the nineteenth day, always for twelve months, sees the seven worlds.
He gains the highest place, served by hosts of apsarases, and a car bright as the sun, sung to by gandharvas.
There he rejoices with excellent immortal women, free from fever, wearing divine robes and glorious, for a hundred ayutas of years.
One who eats once on the full twentieth day, always for twelve months, truthful and firm in vows,
not eating meat, celibate, devoted to the good of all beings, attains the vast divine worlds of the Adityas.
Gandharvas and apsarases with divine garlands and unguents follow him from behind in golden divine cars.
One who eats once on the twenty-first day, always for twelve months, offering to Agni Jatavedas,
goes to the divine world of Ushanas and to Shakra's world, always delighting in the pleasures of the Ashvins and the Maruts.
Ignorant of sorrows, seated in an excellent car, served by excellent women, the lord plays like an immortal.
One who eats once on the twenty-second day, always for twelve months, offering to Agni Jatavedas,
steadfast, devoted to non-harm, truthful and free of envy, attains the worlds of the Vasus, radiant as the sun.
Moving at will, living on nectar, seated in an excellent car, he delights with divine maidens, adorned with divine ornaments.
One who eats once on the twenty-third day, always for twelve months, moderate in food and master of his senses,
goes to the world of Vayu and Ushanas and to Rudra's world, moving and going at will and honoured by hosts of apsarases.
Seated in an excellent car with many good qualities, he delights with divine maidens, adorned with divine ornaments.
One who eats once on the twenty-fourth day, always for twelve months, offering to Agni Jatavedas,
rejoicing, lives long in the abode of the Adityas, wearing divine garlands and robes and anointed with divine scents.
In a divine, charming golden car yoked with swans, he delights with thousands and myriads of divine maidens.
One who eats once on the twenty-fifth day, always for twelve months, mounts a splendid vehicle.
He is followed from behind by chariots yoked with lions and tigers, thundering like clouds, with the sound of Nandi's drums,
ridden by divine maidens, silver, spotless and fair, having mounted a divine and most charming car.
There he lives a thousand kalpas surrounded by hundreds of women, living on the essence of nectar, supreme, like ambrosia.
One who eats once on the twenty-sixth day, always for twelve months, restrained and restrained in food,
master of his senses, free of passion, offering to Agni Jatavedas, attains greatness, honoured by hosts of apsarases.
He gains the worlds of the seven Maruts and of the Vasus too, in a divine crystal car adorned with all jewels.
Honoured by gandharvas and apsarases, he rejoices for two thousand yugas with divine radiance.
One who eats once on the twenty-seventh day, always for twelve months, offering to Agni Jatavedas,
obtains vast fruit and is honoured in the world of the gods; living there on nectar, he rejoices, fully sated.
O king, seated in an excellent car, he dwells in the place frequented by divine sages and royal sages, divine of soul.
Delighting with charming women, proud and excited, he dwells happily three thousand yugas and kalpas.
One who eats once on the twenty-eighth day, always for twelve months, self-controlled and master of his senses,
obtains the vast fruit frequented by divine sages, enjoys pleasures, and shines with splendour like the spotless thousand-rayed sun.
Delicate women of fine radiance, with full breasts and thighs, adorned with divine ornaments, delight him.
They delight him, beloved of heart, in a car like the sun, divine and going wherever one wishes, for a hundred ayutas of kalpa-years.
One who eats once on the twenty-ninth day, always for twelve months, devoted to truthful vows,
has fair, divine worlds honoured by gods and royal sages, and reaches a divine car bright as the moon.
It is made of gold, well yoked, adorned with all jewels, full of hosts of apsarases and resounding with gandharvas.
There fair women adorned with divine ornaments, charming, sweet and ardent, delight him.
Enjoying pleasures, endowed with splendour, bright as Vaishvanara, divine, shining with a divine form like an immortal,
he goes to the worlds of the Vasus, the Maruts, the Sadhyas, the Ashvins and the Rudras, and to Brahma's world.
One who, serene in soul, eats one meal when a month has passed, always for twelve months, would attain Brahma's world.
Fed on the essence of nectar, glorious and charming to all, he shines with splendour, form and beauty like one with rays.
Wearing divine garlands and robes, anointed with divine scents, devoted to pleasures, a yogin ignorant of sorrows,
seated in his car he is honoured by self-radiant women, and constantly worshipped by Rudra's and the divine sages' maidens.
By women of many fair forms and many passions, of many sweet speeches and many delights,
in a car shaped like a city, bright as the sun, behind like the moon, to the north like a cloud,
red to the south, a blue circle below, above resembling varied colours, he lives alone, honoured.
As many years as there are in a thousand years of rain falling on Jambudvipa, so many years are declared for the wise one of Brahma's world.
As many drops as fall from the sky in the rainy season, so long does he dwell, radiant as an immortal.
One who fasts a month at a time, after ten years attains the highest heaven; having reached the state of a great sage, he goes with his body.
The brahmin entered the city gate at the same time, and then, seeing the corpse, suddenly turned back.
Having said this much and taken the king's leave, he was told "So be it" by Kunti's son, and went to the forest.
Those two whom you praise, who were held the only two maharathas among the Vrishni heroes, Pradyumna and Yuyudhana, do you speak of them?
With Dhritarashtra and the illustrious Gandhari, Pandu with his two wives went to Indra's abode.
